blocks.md: Correlated subquery = parameterized inner query. For each outer row, inner query runs with outer row's values as parameters. Powerful but can be slow — consider JOIN or LATERAL for performance.

sections.title: LATERAL Joins — Correlated Subquery in FROM

blocks.label: lateral basics
blocks.code:
-- For each employee, get latest order
SELECT e.name, o.order_date, o.total
FROM employees e
LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT order_date, total
  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.emp_id = e.id
  ORDER BY o.order_date DESC
  LIMIT 1
) o ON true;

-- Equivalent correlated subquery (less readable)
SELECT e.name,
  (SELECT order_date FROM orders o WHERE o.emp_id = e.id ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 1) AS latest_date,
  (SELECT total FROM orders o WHERE o.emp_id = e.id ORDER BY order_date DESC LIMIT 1) AS latest_total
FROM employees e;
blocks.py-pandas:
# GroupBy + head(1)

options: CROSS = inner (drops left rows with no match), LEFT = preserves left
items.explain: CROSS JOIN LATERAL = INNER JOIN LATERAL. LEFT JOIN LATERAL preserves left rows (NULL if no match).

blocks.md: CTE = optimization fence (materialized) by default in PG < 12. NOT MATERIALIZED allows predicate pushdown but may recompute. Use wisely!

items.explain: NOT MATERIALIZED = inline CTE, allowing outer predicates to push into CTE scan.

items.q: A CTE that calls a volatile function such as random() is:
items.explain: Volatile functions force materialization to ensure consistent results per execution.

sections.title: Recursive CTE Patterns — Graphs, Trees, Paths

blocks.label: recursive patterns
blocks.code:
-- Path enumeration: find path from A to B
WITH RECURSIVE paths AS (
  SELECT id, name, ARRAY[id] AS path, 1 AS depth
  FROM nodes WHERE id = 'A'

  UNION ALL

  SELECT n.id, n.name, p.path || n.id, p.depth + 1
  FROM nodes n
  JOIN paths p ON n.parent_id = p.id
  WHERE n.id != ALL(p.path)  -- prevent cycles
  AND p.depth < 10
)
SELECT * FROM paths WHERE id = 'B';

-- Level-order traversal (breadth-first)
WITH RECURSIVE bfs AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS level
  FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL

  UNION ALL

  SELECT e.id, e.name, b.level + 1
  FROM employees e
  JOIN bfs b ON e.manager_id = b.id
)
SELECT * FROM bfs ORDER BY level;

blocks.md: Always include cycle detection (visited set) and max depth limit. Infinite recursion = hung query.

revisionCard: Correlated subquery: runs per outer row; use EXISTS for semi-join, LATERAL for set results
LATERAL: right side sees left columns; CROSS JOIN LATERAL = inner, LEFT JOIN LATERAL = outer
EXISTS stops at first match; IN may scan all. Use EXISTS for correlated semi/anti joins
CTE: NOT MATERIALIZED for pushdown, MATERIALIZED to force; recursive = anchor + UNION ALL + recurse
Recursive CTE: track visited (path array), limit depth, prevent cycles
NOT IN + NULL = zero rows; always NOT EXISTS for anti-join

glossary.def: Subquery referencing outer query columns; executes once per outer row.
Right subquery references left-side columns. Like correlated subquery in FROM.
PostgreSQL hint to inline CTE, enabling predicate pushdown.
CTE with RECURSIVE keyword: anchor + UNION ALL + recursive part referencing itself.
Tracking visited nodes in recursive CTE to prevent infinite loops (path array check).
EXISTS/IN pattern — returns left rows with match; stops at first match per row.
